title: The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5
authors: de Grey, Aubrey D. N. J.
why: First finite non-4-colourable unit-distance graph; every later 5-chromatic record is a reduction of this construction.
facts: smallest exhibited graph has 1581 vertices (abstract; Fig. 9)
the wheel H has 7 vertices and 12 edges, and L contains 52 copies of H (S1 and S3)
M contains a copy of H with no 4-colouring in which that H has a monochromatic triple (S1)

title: Computing Small Unit-Distance Graphs with Chromatic Number 5
why: Turns the 1581-vertex existence proof into SAT-trimmed 553-vertex graphs with mechanically checkable proofs.
facts: produces several 553-vertex 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs (abstract)
the reduction is clausal-proof minimization applied to a 1581-vertex seed (abstract)

title: Trimming Graphs Using Clausal Proof Optimization
why: The proof-optimization method that produced the 529-vertex record; the direct predecessor of Parts' 509.
facts: reduces 553 vertices / 2720 edges to 529 vertices / 2670 edges (abstract)

title: Graph minimization, focusing on the example of 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs in the plane
why: Holds the current 509-vertex record and documents the minimization pipeline that found it.
facts: 509 vertices and 2442 edges (abstract; Table 1)
the graph splits into 374 vertices / 1860 edges plus 136 vertices / 564 edges (S6)
the previous 510-vertex graph has 2502 edges (Table 1)

title: A small 6-chromatic two-distance graph in the plane
why: A 16-vertex 6-chromatic graph for two distances; the smallest known target for a level-5 virtual edge.
facts: 16 vertices, symmetry group of order 48, 28 edges of length 1 and 28 of length d = (sqrt(5)+1)/2 (S2)
the theorem proved is chi(phi) >= 6 (Theorem, after S2)

title: The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5 - a new proof
why: Human-scale alternative to de Grey's computer construction, via a forced equal pair in G40.
facts: G40 has 40 points, 82 unit edges and 59 pairs at distance 8/3 (S2)
G79 has 79 points and 165 unit edges (S2, after Claim 2.1)

title: A 6-chromatic two-distance graph in the plane
why: The 426-vertex 6-chromatic two-distance graph, the other known target for replacing a non-unit edge.
facts: K has 426 vertices, 2009 edges of length 1 and 892 edges of length 2 (S2, after Claim 2.2)
every 5-colouring of K forces A, B and B' to receive the same colour; AB = AB' = 5 and BB' = 1, so chi(K) >= 6 (S2)

title: What percent of the plane can be properly 5- and 6-colored?
why: The tiling/density source of the 6993-vertex lower bound for 7-chromatic graphs.
facts: any unit-distance graph of order at most 6992 is 6-colourable (abstract)
any unit-distance graph of order at most 24 is 5-colourable (abstract)
the 6-colouring covers more than 99.985698% of the plane (abstract)

title: On lower bounds of the order of k-chromatic unit distance graphs
authors: de Grey, Aubrey D. N. J.
why: States the refined numerical bound used to kill the 509-plus-gadget route: v7 > 6992.
facts: the finite upper bounds are v5 <= 509 and e5 <= 2406 (S1, footnote 2)

title: The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable
why: Raises the plane lower bound to 6, leaving exactly the 6-versus-7 question; the proof is infinitary and gives no finite witness.
facts: Theorem 1.1: there is no proper 5-colouring of R^2, even with arbitrary colour classes; hence 6 <= chi(R^2) <= 7 (p. 2)
the proof works in ZFC and transfers arbitrary colourings to weak measurable ones (Theorems 1.3 and 1.4)
no finite vertex set or edge list is produced (the paper says the graph and constant are existential)

title: The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable - Lean 4 formalization
why: Machine-checked version of the infinitary theorem; also the evidence that no finite witness can be extracted from it.
facts: Five.lean is 131 lines with 0 occurrences of `sorry`
`theorem no_proper_five_coloring : not exists c : C -> Fin 5, ProperColoring 5 c` is at line 124
the file proves the statement for the continuum C, not for a finite `Fin N` vertex set

title: Planar unit distances - Lean 4 formalization of a sub-4/3 exponent
why: The unit-distance counting problem is the quantitative sibling of Hadwiger-Nelson; this is the first sub-3/2 exponent with a formal proof, not a full resolution.
facts: Main.lean is 137 lines with 0 occurrences of `sorry`
`theorem main : exists C beta : R, 0 < C and 1 <= beta and beta < 4/3 and forall n, u n <= C * n^beta` (lines 129-131)
this is a sub-4/3 exponent, a power saving over the trivial O(n^{3/2}) bound, but not the conjectured n^{1+o(1)}

title: Polymath16 wiki: Hadwiger-Nelson problem
why: The community ledger of vertex/edge counts and gadget definitions that the papers omit.
facts: table: G has 1581 vertices / 7877 edges and G0 has 1585 / 7909
L has 121 vertices / 301 edges and M has 1345 / 8268
the diamond is 4 vertices / 5 edges and the Moser spindle is 7 / 11

title: A 14-vertex 6-chromatic distance graph in the Euclidean plane (prescribed distances 1, 1/sqrt3, 2)
why: The smallest known 6-chromatic graph for three prescribed distances; a concrete calibration object below 509 vertices.
facts: G14 has 14 vertices and 50 edges: 18 of length 1, 27 of length 1/sqrt3, 5 of length 2 (README table)
chi(G14) = 6 and omega(G14) = 4; the distance triple admits no K5 anywhere in the plane (README)
no 13-point witness exists, so 14 is minimum (README, main result 3)

title: The Falconer distance conjecture in all dimensions
why: A distance-set problem in the same circle as Hadwiger-Nelson, resolved in full and with a quantitative threshold.
facts: Theorem 1.1: for every integer d >= 2 and compact E in R^d, dim_H E > d/2 implies the distance set of E has positive Lebesgue measure
the threshold d/2 is sharp and no regularity beyond Hausdorff dimension is assumed

title: Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions
why: A 2025 resolution of a major incidence/geometry conjecture; the technique (tube volume estimates) is the closest transferable machinery to distance-set bounds.
facts: every Kakeya set in R^3 has Minkowski and Hausdorff dimension 3 (abstract)

title: de Grey Graphs
why: Records the dimension-3 state of the art, where 6-chromatic graphs are explicit but 5-chromatic triangle-free examples appear only in 2026.
facts: 59- and 60-vertex unit-distance graphs in R^3 have chromatic number 6
a 61-vertex triangle-free unit-distance graph in R^3 has chromatic number 5
the plane record listed is still the 2131-vertex spindle-free graph

title: Measurable Chromatic Number of the Plane
why: The measurable variant is the standard test of whether an unrestricted colouring argument can be made geometric; Falconer's bound is its founding result.
facts: surveys the measurable chromatic number chi_m(R^2), with Falconer's 1981 lower bound chi_m(R^2) >= 5
the unrestricted and measurable numbers are not known to coincide; both lie between 5 and 7

title: Ganze Cremona-Transformationen
why: The origin of the problem: polynomial self-maps with constant non-zero Jacobian determinant.
facts: poses the question for polynomial maps F : C^n -> C^n with det JF in C*; such maps are now called Keller maps
the planar case JC(2) is still open

title: A Jacobian criterion for separability
why: The first degree bound: degree 2 is settled in every dimension, so all counterexample searches start at degree 3.
facts: every Keller map of total degree <= 2 is invertible, in every dimension (main theorem)

title: On the Jacobian conjecture and the configurations of roots
why: The degree-100 wall, the first bound obtained by Newton-polygon/root-configuration analysis.
facts: a planar Keller counterexample must have total degree > 100 (main theorem)

title: An effective approach to Keller's Jacobian Conjecture
why: Reduces the whole conjecture to cubic-linear maps, the standard finite-dimensional reduction used by later searches.
facts: reduces JC(n) to maps of the form F = x + (Ax)^{*3} with A nilpotent (cubic-linear reduction)

title: Lectures on Expansion Techniques in Algebraic Geometry
why: The valuation/Newton-polygon dictionary for Keller pairs; the source of the two-points-at-infinity constraint.
facts: Theorem (19.4): JC is equivalent to each of k[f,g]=A, f having one point at infinity, N(f) being a triangle, and deg f | deg g or deg g | deg f
every component of a Keller pair has at most two points at infinity (Theorem 18.13, used in 19.4)

title: Polynomial derivations and their rings of constants
why: The derivation-side formulation: rings of constants and the local nilpotence criteria that make JC equivalent to a statement about derivations.
facts: monograph (1994) on derivations of k[x_1,...,x_n] and their rings of constants
the Nowicki conjecture on Weitzenboeck derivations is posed in this setting

title: Polynomial Automorphisms and the Jacobian Conjecture
why: The standard monograph: normal forms, reductions, and the equivalence list that every Jacobian search uses.
facts: second edition, Frontiers in Mathematics (Birkhaeuser, 2021); first edition 2000
the monograph treats Keller maps, the degree reduction, and the derivation/Dixmier reformulations

title: A reduction of the Jacobian Conjecture to the symmetric case
why: Shows the conjecture can be tested on symmetric Jacobian matrices, shrinking the coefficient space of any search.
facts: reduces JC to the case in which the Jacobian matrix is symmetric (main theorem)

title: Some algorithms related to the Jacobian Conjecture
why: The only published Newton-polygon corner enumerator; it defines the admissible search space below degree 150.
facts: enumerates all possible corners for gcd(deg P, deg Q) <= 35 (abstract)
enumerates all degree pairs with max(deg P, deg Q) <= 150 (abstract)

title: Increasing the degree of a possible counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture from 100 to 108
why: The (72,108) reduction: below degree 125 only this pair survives, with exactly two Newton-polygon configurations.
facts: Theorem 2.1: max{deg P, deg Q} >= 125, or (deg P, deg Q) is (72,108) or (108,72)
Proposition 4.3 lists exactly two configurations: N(P)={(0,0),(1,0),(8,14),(8,16),(0,8)} and N(Q)={(0,0),(2,1),(12,21),(12,24),(0,12)} for (1), and the four-corner versions for (2)
the proved lower bound rises from 100 to 108, not to 125 (abstract)

title: The Alpoge-Fable counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture: verification, geometry, dynamics, and an equivariant program for the plane case
why: Independent verification and geometric analysis of the July 2026 C^3 counterexample; the reference object for the non-planar case.
facts: F = (u^3 z + y^2 u(4+3xy), y + 3x u^2 z + 3x y^2(4+3xy), 2x - 3x^2 y - x^3 z) with u = 1+xy has det DF = -2 identically (p. 1)
the fibres have geometric degree 3 and full S_3 monodromy (abstract)

title: A digestion of the Jacobian conjecture counterexample
why: The clearest derivation of where the C^3 map comes from; reconstructs it as a resultant of a linear and a quadratic polynomial.
facts: the construction is a homogeneous resultant of a linear polynomial and a quadratic polynomial
the resulting polynomial has degree seven
the post records the component degrees 7, 6 and 4

title: The new counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture
why: The algebraic-geometry reading of the counterexample: elimination to a cubic relation, and a separate 24-variable det = 1 construction in the comments.
facts: eliminating any two variables produces a cubic relation in the remaining one
the comments record a separate 2026 cubic-homogeneous map in 24 variables with det(DG) = 1 and a rational collision

title: The plane (72,108) Jacobian case - an independent structural proof
why: Claims to close both (72,108) configurations, which would raise the plane degree bound to 125; unrefereed but with executable checkers.
facts: Theorem A: no (P,Q) in K[x,x^-1,y]^2 with [P,Q]=x^2 and either configuration (1) or configuration (2) of GGHV 2022, Proposition 4.3
Corollary B: conditional on two stated inputs, every plane counterexample has max{deg P, deg Q} >= 125
the README attributes priority for the exclusion to Helali, Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21479814

title: Jacobian conjecture, two-dimensional case
why: A complete classification of planar Keller pairs of total degree at most 3, which makes the low-degree box provably empty.
facts: classifies all Keller pairs of total degree <= 3 up to linear conjugacy (main theorem)
the normal form is (x + a2 s^2 + a3 s^3, y - a2 s^2 - a3 s^3) with s = x+y and determinant 1

title: Structure of Keller mappings, two-dimensional case
why: Extends the classification to degree 4 and exhibits the first non-triangular tame families, calibrating what a counterexample must not look like.
facts: classifies Keller pairs of total degree <= 4 (main theorem)
exhibits F_{c,s} = (x + c y^2, y - s x^2 - 2cs x y^2 - c^2 s y^4) with c,s non-zero and determinant 1

title: Some classes satisfying the 2-dimensional Jacobian conjecture and a proof of the complex conjecture until degree 104
why: The current unconditional degree wall for JC(2): 104, four above Moh's 100.
facts: proves the complex two-dimensional Jacobian conjecture for total degree <= 104 (abstract)
improves Moh's 1983 bound of 100 (abstract)

title: Sur les algebres de Weyl
why: The non-commutative sibling: endomorphisms of the Weyl algebra, equivalent to JC in the stable range and open in every dimension.
facts: poses the endomorphism problem for the Weyl algebra A_n(C)
Dixmier(n) is equivalent to JC(n) for the same n (Tsuchimoto; Belov-Kanel-Kontsevich)

title: A Dimension-Two Counterexample to the Separable Jacobian Conjecture in Characteristic Two
why: A clean solved analogue: the separable Jacobian conjecture is false in characteristic 2, in dimension 2, with an explicit degree-3 collision.
facts: over the algebraic closure of F_2, F = (x + x^2 y + x^4 + x^6 y^2, y + x^5 + x^6 y + x^7 y^2 + x^8 y^3) has det JF = 1
the three distinct points (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) have the same image
the function-field extension has degree 3 and is separable

title: The tame and the wild automorphisms of polynomial rings in three variables
why: A solved structural analogue: the tame generators problem, open for decades, was settled negatively in dimension 3.
facts: proves that Aut(k[x,y,z]) contains wild automorphisms (main theorem)
the tame generators problem has a negative answer in dimension 3

title: Mathieu-Zhao Spaces and the Jacobian Conjecture
why: The Mathieu-Zhao reformulation is the widest currently open statement that JC is known to imply.
facts: survey chapter (2020) connecting Mathieu-Zhao subspaces to the Jacobian conjecture
records the implication JC => Mathieu conjecture for the appropriate class of maps

title: A proof of the two-dimensional Markus-Yamabe Stability Conjecture and a generalization
why: The dynamical analogue of JC(2) that *is* true: a global-stability statement for planar polynomial vector fields.
facts: proves the Markus-Yamabe conjecture in dimension 2: a local diffeomorphism of R^2 whose Jacobian has negative trace everywhere has 0 as a global attractor (abstract)

title: A Polynomial Counterexample to the Markus-Yamabe Conjecture
why: Shows the dimension-2 Markus-Yamabe theorem does not lift: the polynomial counterexample appears already in dimension 3.
facts: exhibits a polynomial counterexample to Markus-Yamabe in dimension 3
the planar theorem therefore does not generalise to n >= 3

title: Notes on elliptic curves. II.
why: The conjecture itself, in the form the terminal object must refute: analytic order of vanishing equals Mordell-Weil rank.
facts: conjecture: ord_{s=1} L(E,s) = rank E(Q)
the leading coefficient is predicted as a product of the real period, regulator, |Sha|, Tamagawa numbers and torsion

title: Heegner points and derivatives of L-series
why: The rank-1 half of BSD: the first derivative is an explicit multiple of the height of a Heegner point.
facts: proves L'(E,1) equals an explicit non-zero constant times the canonical height of a Heegner point (rank 1)
together with the rank-0 case this gives BSD for analytic rank <= 1 once Sha is controlled

title: Euler Systems
why: The other half of Gross-Zagier-Kolyvagin: an Euler system bounds the Selmer group, so analytic rank <= 1 forces the algebraic rank.
facts: introduces Euler systems and applies them to Heegner points on modular elliptic curves
for analytic rank <= 1, the Mordell-Weil rank equals the analytic rank and Sha is finite

title: Explicit Heegner Points: Kolyvagin's Conjecture and Non-trivial Elements in the Shafarevich-Tate Group
why: The precise citation for the GZK gate and for the rank >= 2 Selmer corank statement that rules out the easy counterexample shapes.
facts: Theorem 1.1 (Gross-Zagier, Kolyvagin): if r_an(E/Q) <= 1 then r_an(E/Q) = r_MW(E/Q)
Kolyvagin's conjecture implies that analytic rank >= 2 forces Z_p-corank Sel_p >= 2 (abstract)

title: Proving the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for specific elliptic curves of analytic rank zero and one
why: The largest published pointwise verification in the GZK range; calibrates how far 'checked' actually extends.
facts: proves BSD for 16,714 of the 16,725 curves of conductor < 5000 with analytic rank 0 or 1 (abstract)

title: LMFDB - Reliability of L-function data
why: Establishes that analytic ranks above 1 are rigorously certified in the database, which invalidates 'k >= 2 is not certifiable'.
facts: for classical modular form L-functions the displayed analytic rank has been rigorously verified in all cases, including rank > 1 (page text)
for any displayed analytic rank r <= 1 the value must be correct (page text)

title: LMFDB - Completeness of elliptic curve data over Q
why: Defines the region where a rank mismatch is impossible by construction, and hence the only region worth sweeping.
facts: the database contains all curves of conductor < 500,000 (page text)
it contains 3,824,372 curves in 2,917,287 isogeny classes, with maximum conductor 299,996,953 (page text)
it also contains all 7-smooth conductors and all prime conductors <= 300,000,000

title: Elliptic curves by rank
why: The rank-record tables that supply calibration curves for any certified-rank pipeline.
facts: rank 4 record: conductor 234,446, curve [1,-1,0,-79,289]
rank 5 record: conductor 19,047,851, curve [0,0,1,-79,342]
rank 6 record: conductor 5,187,563,742, curve [1,1,0,-2582,48720]

title: Curves D y^2 = x^3 - x of odd analytic rank
why: A large explicit family where odd analytic rank is proved and BSD then predicts positive rank; the standard congruent-number computation.
facts: proves positive rank for every |D| < 10^6 with |D| congruent to 5, 6 or 7 mod 8 (abstract)
the proof uses Heegner points from CM points on modular curves and a numerical height check

title: Binary quartic forms having bounded invariants, and the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves
why: The strongest unconditional average-rank bound; it is why a random curve is not where a counterexample will be found.
facts: the mean size of the 2-Selmer group, ordered by height, is 3 (abstract)
consequently limsup of the average rank is at most 1.5 (abstract)

title: The class number of quadratic fields and the conjectures of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer
why: The bridge that made the class-number problem a corollary of an analytic-rank statement, later closed by Gross-Zagier.
facts: reduces the effective class-number problem for imaginary quadratic fields to the existence of an elliptic curve with a zero of order >= 3 at s = 1
Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa, series 4, volume 3 (1976), pages 623-663

title: Congruent Numbers and Heegner Points
why: The congruent-number problem is the cleanest conditional corollary of BSD; Tian's Heegner-point construction gives unconditional families.
facts: constructs Heegner points on m y^2 = x^3 - x for integers m with many prime divisors (abstract)
extends Heegner's prime-conductor construction to composite m

title: A Family of Calabi-Yau Varieties and Potential Automorphy II
why: Sato-Tate is the model 'local-statistics' theorem: a conjecture about every elliptic curve, proved by potential automorphy.
facts: proves potential automorphy for a family of Calabi-Yau varieties (main theorem)
this yields the Sato-Tate conjecture for elliptic curves over Q

title: Modular Elliptic Curves and Fermat's Last Theorem
why: The canonical 'big theorem with a complete method' case: modularity of semistable curves, then FLT as a corollary.
facts: proves that every semistable elliptic curve over Q is modular (main theorem)
deduces Fermat's Last Theorem for all exponents >= 3

title: The DRAT format and DRAT-trim checker
why: The certificate format behind every claimed unit-distance lower bound; a SAT answer without a DRAT/LRAT trace is not a proof.
facts: DRAT extends RUP with the RAT rule and is checkable in polynomial time per step (abstract)
DRAT-trim is the reference checker described in the paper

title: Computational methods and experiments in analytic number theory
why: The practical reference for the approximate functional equation and for rigorous zero-counting of L-functions.
facts: surveys summation by parts, Euler-Maclaurin summation, Poisson summation and the FFT for evaluating L-functions (abstract)
also covers conjectures and experiments connecting number theory and random matrix theory (abstract)

title: Computing special values of motivic L-functions
why: The algorithm that turns a functional equation into certified numerical L-values and Taylor coefficients.
facts: computes L-values and Taylor coefficients from a smoothed approximate functional equation (abstract)
the method applies to motivic L-functions with a known functional equation

title: Arb: Efficient Arbitrary-Precision Midpoint-Radius Interval Arithmetic
why: The interval backend that makes a numerical analytic rank into a certified statement rather than a tolerance test.
facts: implements midpoint-radius interval arithmetic with rigorous error bounds (abstract)
supports arbitrary-precision special functions used in L-function evaluation

title: Every planar map is four colorable
why: The first machine-assisted colouring theorem: a finite discharging argument plus a computer check of 1,936 reducible configurations.
facts: Theorem: every planar map can be coloured with at most four colours (abstract)
the proof reduced the problem to 1,936 configurations checked by computer

title: The Four-Colour Theorem
why: A simplified, independently checked proof of the four-colour theorem; the model for a colouring proof with a small finite kernel.
facts: gives a new proof of the four-colour theorem
the reducibility part uses 633 configurations

title: The Four Colour Theorem: Engineering of a Formal Proof
why: The Coq formalization of the four-colour theorem: the closest existing model for a machine-checked colouring proof.
facts: the four-colour theorem was formalized and machine-checked in Coq
the formalization covers both the discharging and the reducibility parts

title: Every Planar Map is Four Colorable
why: The book-length account of the original four-colour proof, including the full configuration list that the announcement omits.
facts: the AMS volume is the full account of the 1,936-configuration proof (1989)

title: A proof of the Kepler conjecture
why: A second computer-assisted geometry proof with a huge finite case check; the template for Flyspeck.
facts: every packing of congruent balls in R^3 has density at most pi/(3*sqrt(2)) = 0.74048... (main theorem)

title: A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture
why: Flyspeck: the completed formal proof of Kepler in HOL Light and Isabelle, the largest formalized geometry proof before 2020.
facts: the proof is formalized in a combination of HOL Light and Isabelle (abstract)
the paper is the official account of the completed Flyspeck project (abstract)

title: Solving and Verifying the Boolean Pythagorean Triples Problem via Cube-and-Conquer
why: The canonical SAT proof of a Ramsey-type colouring statement, with a 200 TB DRAT certificate; the closest scale analogue to a 6,993-vertex colouring proof.
facts: the set {1,...,7825} cannot be 2-coloured without a monochromatic Pythagorean triple (main theorem)
the set {1,...,7824} can be so coloured, so 7825 is sharp
the DRAT certificate is about 200 TB

title: A SAT Attack on the Erdős Discrepancy Conjecture
why: A SAT refutation of a famous infinite combinatorics conjecture, with the exact finite threshold; the model for turning an infinite statement into one SAT instance.
facts: there is a +/-1 sequence of length 1160 with discrepancy at most 2, but none of length 1161 (main theorem)

title: DRAT-trim: Efficient Checking and Trimming Using Expressive Clausal Proofs
why: The reference checker for DRAT proofs and the tool that makes a SAT lower bound independently verifiable.
facts: DRAT-trim checks DRAT clausal proofs and trims them to a smaller core (abstract)
it is the checker used for the 200 TB Boolean Pythagorean triples certificate

title: Efficient Certified RAT Verification
why: cake_lpr: a formally verified RAT checker, the independent second checker a DRAT claim needs.
facts: presents cake_lpr, a formally verified checker for RAT proofs in CakeML (abstract)

title: House of Graphs: A database of interesting graphs
why: The public graph database used to distribute and search for extremal colouring graphs; a place to look for seeds the papers do not print.
facts: House of Graphs is a searchable database of graphs with invariants and canonical augmentation (abstract)
it supports uploading and searching graphs by invariant

title: The Mathematical Coloring Book
why: The historical and mathematical reference for the Hadwiger-Nelson problem, including the pre-2018 bounds and the measurable variant.
facts: the book surveys the Hadwiger-Nelson problem; at publication the bounds were 4 <= chi(R^2) <= 7
it contains the history of the problem and the measurable chromatic number

title: A 15-colouring of 3-space omitting distance one
why: The upper bound chi(R^3) <= 15: a dimension-3 colouring that the plane analogue does not have.
facts: gives a 15-colouring of R^3 with no two points at distance 1 in the same class (title theorem)

title: On the space chromatic number
why: The explicit 6-chromatic lower bound for R^3, which shows dimension 3 is strictly easier than the plane for constructions.
facts: proves chi(R^3) >= 6

title: Axiom of choice and chromatic number of the plane
why: Shows the de Bruijn-Erdos compactness step can fail without choice; a finite-witness claim must say which set theory it is proved in.
facts: in ZF, the chromatic number of the plane need not equal the supremum of the chromatic numbers of its finite subgraphs

title: Unit Distance Graphs with Ambiguous Chromatic Number
why: Constructs unit-distance graphs on R^n whose chromatic number depends on the axioms, sharpening the foundational caveat for the plane.
facts: constructs unit-distance graphs on R^n whose chromatic number depends on the axioms of set theory (abstract)

title: Polymath16, first thread: Simplifying de Grey's graph
why: The working log of the reduction race; records the vertex counts at each stage, including the 1577 record before the corrected 1581.
facts: thread 1 posted 2018-04-14; the current record at that time was 1577 vertices
lists the project goals: smaller 5-chromatic graphs, human-verifiable proofs, and a 6-chromatic search

title: Unit-Distance Graph
why: A compact, current table of the smallest known unit-distance graphs and their chromatic numbers.
facts: the smallest 4-chromatic unit-distance graph is the Moser spindle, with 7 vertices and 11 edges
the page records 4 <= chi(R^2) <= 7 and the standard graph families

title: epsilon-Unit Distance Graphs
why: Shows the exact-distance problem is a knife-edge: allow an epsilon slack and the chromatic number jumps to 7 for a range of epsilon.
facts: for certain epsilon, the epsilon-unit distance graph has chromatic number exactly 7 (abstract)
for smaller epsilon the lower bound is at least 5 (abstract)

title: Axiom of choice and chromatic number: examples on the plane
why: Gives plane examples of the axiom-dependence, not just abstract graphs; the sharpest warning that a finite-witness argument is not choice-free.
facts: constructs examples on the plane of graphs whose chromatic number depends on the axiom of choice (title)

title: A counterexample to the strong real Jacobian conjecture
why: The single best solved analogue: the real Jacobian conjecture is false in dimension 2, with an explicit polynomial map whose Jacobian is positive everywhere and which is not injective.
facts: there is a polynomial map R^2 -> R^2 with det J > 0 at every point that is not injective (main theorem)

title: The Jacobian conjecture: Reduction of degree and formal expansion of the inverse
why: The degree-3 reduction that every later Jacobian search uses; without it the coefficient space is unbounded.
facts: reduces JC(n) to the case F = x + H with H homogeneous of degree 3 and JH nilpotent (Reduction Theorem)
introduces the formal inverse and the tree expansion used by later degree bounds

title: Keller's problem
why: An independent cubic reduction of the Jacobian problem, contemporaneous with Bass-Connell-Wright.
facts: gives a reduction of Keller's problem to cubic polynomial maps (1980)

title: Homogeneous Keller maps
why: The systematic study of homogeneous Keller maps and nilpotent Jacobians; the source for the low-dimensional classifications a search should not redo.
facts: 349-page PhD thesis (Radboud University Nijmegen, defended 7 July 2009)
classifies homogeneous quasi-translations and nilpotent Jacobians in dimensions 3-5

title: The Jacobian Conjecture is Stably Equivalent to the Dixmier Conjecture
why: The precise equivalence between the Jacobian and Dixmier problems; it tells you which non-commutative formulation is a fair substitute.
facts: JC(2n) implies Dixmier(n), so the stable Jacobian and Dixmier conjectures are equivalent (abstract)

title: Mathieu subspaces of associative algebras
why: Defines the Mathieu-Zhao spaces that make the Mathieu conjecture a Jacobian-adjacent statement; the widest open target JC implies.
facts: introduces Mathieu subspaces of associative algebras (title and main definition)
the Mathieu conjecture becomes the statement that the image of a polynomial map is a Mathieu subspace

title: Characteristic p approaches to the Jacobian conjecture
why: The characteristic-p side of the problem, where the conjecture is false and the counterexamples are explicit; a source of structural obstructions.
facts: surveys characteristic-p approaches to the Jacobian conjecture (2024)

title: New classes of polynomial maps satisfying the real Jacobian conjecture in R^2
why: Real JC is true on two explicit families, even though Pinchuk shows it is false in general; the boundary is structural, not degree-based.
facts: the maps (q(x)-p(y), q(y)+p(x)) with p'q' != 0 satisfy the real Jacobian conjecture (abstract)
homogeneous (f,g) of the same degree satisfying the stated conditions also satisfy it (abstract)

title: On three-sheeted polynomial mappings of C^2
why: A geometric-degree wall: no 3-sheeted Keller map. It kills an entire topological degree before any coefficient search.
facts: the Jacobian of a 3-sheeted polynomial mapping C^2 -> C^2 cannot be a non-zero constant (abstract)

title: On four-sheeted polynomial mappings of C^2. I. The case of an irreducible ramification curve
why: Extends the geometric-degree wall to 4 sheets under the irreducible-ramification hypothesis; a negative result that narrows the topological search.
facts: no 4-sheeted Keller map with one dicritical component (main theorem)

title: On four-sheeted polynomial mappings of C^2. The general case
why: The general 4-sheeted exclusion, completing the geometric-degree wall below 5.
facts: completes the exclusion of 4-sheeted Keller maps of C^2 (general case)

title: An application of Newton-Puiseux charts to the Jacobian problem
why: Uses Newton-Puiseux charts to exclude topological degree at most 5; the method is the same edge/valuation cascade the (72,108) work needs.
facts: excludes a Keller map of topological degree at most 5

title: The Jacobian Conjecture: symmetric reduction and solution in the symmetric cubic linear case
why: A solved subcase of the cubic-linear reduction: symmetry plus cubic linearity is enough. It calibrates what a counterexample must break.
facts: proves the symmetric cubic-linear case of the Jacobian conjecture (title)

title: Frameworks for Two-Dimensional Keller Maps
why: Reformulates the 2D Keller map as a finite combinatorial framework; the right shape for a computer search, unlike a raw coefficient system.
facts: reduces a 2D Keller map to a finite set of combinatorial conditions ('frameworks') (abstract)
each framework corresponds to a large system of equations whose solution would give a Keller map (abstract)

title: Pinchuk maps, function fields, and real Jacobian conjectures
why: Explains why Pinchuk's counterexample does not contradict the complex JC: the real maps have degree-6 function-field extensions, not odd degree.
facts: the Pinchuk counterexamples have function-field extensions of degree six with no nontrivial automorphisms (abstract)
a real Jacobian counterexample must have an odd-degree extension with no nontrivial automorphisms (abstract)

title: On the shape of possible counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture
why: The gcd obstruction: every planar counterexample has gcd(deg P, deg Q) >= 16, which eliminates most degree pairs before any algebra.
facts: gives an elementary proof that gcd(deg P, deg Q) >= 16 for any planar counterexample (abstract)
proves gcd(deg P, deg Q) != 2p for any prime p (abstract)

title: Reduction theorems for the Strong Real Jacobian Conjecture
why: Reduces the strong real Jacobian conjecture to specialized forms, delimiting exactly how far Pinchuk's counterexample generalizes.
facts: proves reduction theorems for the strong real Jacobian conjecture (title)

title: Algorithm for determining the type of a singular fiber in an elliptic pencil
why: Tate's algorithm is how the conductor and the local Tamagawa factors are actually computed; without it there is no L-function to evaluate.
facts: gives an algorithm determining the Kodaira type of each singular fibre of an elliptic pencil (title)

title: Algorithms for Modular Elliptic Curves
why: The mwrank book: modular symbols, Tate's algorithm, 2-descent and the rank algorithms the BSD pipeline depends on.
facts: second edition 1997; the author-hosted text is the corrected second edition
covers modular-symbol computation, Tate's algorithm, and 2-descent for elliptic curves over Q

title: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture, a Computational Approach
why: The textbook that connects the BSD conjecture to computation: L-values, Sha, Heegner points, Kolyvagin's Euler system, and verification.
facts: the book has chapters on the BSD rank conjecture, Sha, Heegner points, the Euler system, and computational verification (contents)
the text is 63+ pages and is the source for the Sage BSD algorithms

title: On the Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer quotients modulo squares
why: The parity conjecture: it predicts the sign of the rank and hence rules out half the possible mismatch shapes before any computation.
facts: proves the parity conjecture for elliptic curves assuming finiteness of Sha(E/K)[2] and conditions at 2 and 3 (abstract)
the parity of the Mordell-Weil rank agrees with the parity of the analytic rank (abstract)

title: Conjectures on elliptic curves over quadratic fields
why: The origin of Goldfeld's average-rank conjecture; it is the reason a random curve is not a plausible counterexample.
facts: proposes conjectures on the average rank of elliptic curves over quadratic fields (title)

title: Euler Systems
why: The book-length treatment of Euler systems, the machinery that bounds Selmer groups and supplies the GZK rank theorem.
facts: Euler systems are systems of cohomology classes used to bound Selmer groups (abstract)
they give cases of BSD and of the Iwasawa main conjecture (abstract)

title: Artin's Conjecture, Turing's Method, and the Riemann Hypothesis
why: The rigorous zero-counting reference: Turing's method plus the explicit formula, the technique that turns a numerical analytic rank into a theorem.
facts: presents a group-theoretic criterion for verifying the Artin conjecture up to finite height (abstract)
discusses two methods for locating zeros of arbitrary L-functions, including Turing's method (abstract)

title: Computing degree 1 L-functions rigorously
why: A worked, large-scale implementation of rigorous zero-counting for degree-1 L-functions; the engineering model for certifying k.
facts: verifies the generalized Riemann hypothesis for all characters of modulus q <= 100,000 to height qT >= 10^8 (abstract)
confirms non-vanishing of L_chi(1/2) for all characters of modulus q <= 2,000,000 (abstract)

title: Rapid computation of special values of Dirichlet L-functions
why: The fast, rigorous evaluation layer: p^{3/2+o(1)} bit complexity for zeta and Dirichlet L-values, an order better than the previous p^{2+o(1)}.
facts: computes zeta(s) and L(s,chi) to p-bit accuracy in p^{3/2+o(1)} bit complexity (abstract)
improves the previous p^{2+o(1)} complexity (abstract)

title: Factoring polynomials with rational coefficients
why: LLL: the polynomial-time lattice reduction behind integer relation detection, coefficient recovery, and many exact-arithmetic certificates.
facts: gives a polynomial-time algorithm for lattice basis reduction (main theorem)
applies it to factor polynomials with rational coefficients

title: Analysis of PSLQ, an integer relation finding algorithm
why: PSLQ turns a high-precision numerical identity into an exact integer relation; the standard tool for recovering algebraic coefficients from numerics.
facts: analyzes PSLQ, an integer relation algorithm, and gives its detection thresholds (abstract)
the algorithm runs in polynomial time in the dimension and precision

title: Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms
why: The standard textbook for Groebner bases, resultants and elimination, the machinery behind every coefficient-system computation here.
facts: fourth edition (2015); covers Groebner bases, resultants, and elimination theory
includes the Buchberger algorithm and its applications

title: The complexity of the word problems for commutative semigroups and polynomial ideals
why: The double-exponential lower bound for Groebner bases: a reason not to put a 445-unknown system through naive elimination.
facts: Gröbner basis computation is doubly exponential in the worst case (main theorem)

title: Solving Systems of Polynomial Equations
why: A compact map of the algorithmic options: resultants, Groebner bases, homotopy continuation, and numerical algebraic geometry.
facts: CBMS lectures covering resultants, Groebner bases, and homotopy continuation (contents)
the book is the standard short reference for polynomial system solving

title: The Lean mathematical library
why: The library the OpenAI colouring formalization builds on; its design explains what finite combinatorics is already available and what must be built.
facts: mathlib is a community-driven Lean library with dependent types, a structure hierarchy, and large- and small-scale automation (abstract)

title: Handbook of Satisfiability
why: The reference for SAT encodings, CDCL, symmetry breaking, and proof logging; the engineering base under every HN lower bound.
facts: second edition (2021); covers CDCL, SAT encodings, symmetry breaking, and proof logging

title: Shatter: efficient symmetry-breaking for Boolean satisfiability
why: Symmetry breaking is what makes a 6,993-vertex colouring instance tractable; Shatter is the canonical construction of lex-leader predicates.
facts: gives a linear-sized CNF formula that selects lex-leaders for single permutations (abstract)
adds symmetry-breaking predicates that preserve satisfiability (abstract)

title: Algorithms in Real Algebraic Geometry
why: The reference for Newton-Puiseux expansions and real algebraic algorithms, the symbolic layer under the edge cascade and interval checks.
facts: textbook on algorithms in real algebraic geometry, including Newton-Puiseux expansions and quantifier elimination

title: Undecidability of the spectral gap
why: A negative result that kills a whole route: the spectral gap is undecidable in general, so no algorithm can settle every mass-gap instance.
facts: the spectral gap problem for quantum many-body systems is undecidable (main theorem)

title: Hilbert's Tenth Problem is Unsolvable
why: The canonical undecidability result for Diophantine equations; it bounds what a general algebraic search can be expected to decide.
facts: Hilbert's tenth problem (a general algorithm for Diophantine equations) is unsolvable (main theorem)
